title: What operational documentation does a production service need — a README (what the service does, how to build/run/test it, key dependencies), runbooks for on-call (step-by-step procedures for common alerts like "DB connection pool exhausted" or "Kafka consumer lag > 100K"), troubleshooting guides (how to diagnose common failures with commands and links), deployment documentation (how to deploy, roll back, verify), and architecture diagrams (how this service fits into the bigger system) — and why are runbooks a reliability tool (reduce MTTR, reduce tribal-knowledge dependence, enable any on-call engineer to handle an incident they haven't seen before)?
shortTitle: Operational documentation a production service needs — README, runbooks, troubleshooting guides, deployment docs, architecture diagrams

s1_definition.profdef: Operational documentation is the set of written artifacts that let a team build, deploy, run, and recover a production service without relying on the memory of whoever originally wrote it. The core artifacts are the README (orientation and local setup), runbooks (step-by-step incident procedures triggered by specific alerts), troubleshooting guides (diagnostic recipes for common failures), deployment documentation (how to release, roll back, and verify), and architecture diagrams (how the service connects to the rest of the system). Runbooks in particular are a reliability tool because they convert tribal knowledge into repeatable procedures, which reduces Mean Time To Recovery and lets any on-call engineer act confidently during an incident they have never personally seen.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India branch where Rajesh works. If only one teller knows how to open the vault, the bank is in trouble the day that teller is on holiday. So the bank keeps a binder: how to open for the day, what to do when the ATM jams, who to call when the cash runs low, and a floor map showing where everything is. Operational documentation is that binder for a software service. The runbook is the "ATM jammed — do these five steps" page that any teller can follow at 3 a.m. without phoning the manager.
s1_definition.oneliner: Operational documentation turns "ask the person who built it" into "follow the page," which is the difference between a five-minute recovery and a five-hour outage.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Operational documentation is the set of written artifacts that let a team build, deploy, run, and recover a production service without relying on the memory of whoever originally wrote it. The core artifacts are the README (orientation and local setup), runbooks (step-by-step incident procedures triggered by specific alerts), troubleshooting guides (diagnostic recipes for common failures), deployment documentation (how to release, roll back, and verify), and architecture diagrams (how the service connects to the rest of the system). Runbooks in particular are a reliability tool because they convert tribal knowledge into repeatable procedures, which reduces Mean Time To Recovery and lets any on-call engineer act confidently during an incident they have never personally seen.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India branch where Rajesh works. If only one teller knows how to open the vault, the bank is in trouble the day that teller is on holiday. So the bank keeps a binder: how to open for the day, what to do when the ATM jams, who to call when the cash runs low, and a floor map showing where everything is. Operational documentation is that binder for a software service. The runbook is the "ATM jammed — do these five steps" page that any teller can follow at 3 a.m. without phoning the manager.

**One line to remember:** Operational documentation turns "ask the person who built it" into "follow the page," which is the difference between a five-minute recovery and a five-hour outage.

sections.s2_technical:
A production service needs five distinct kinds of documentation, and each answers a different question. The README answers "what is this and how do I run it locally?" It states what the service does in one or two sentences, lists the key dependencies such as the database, the message broker, and downstream services, and gives the exact commands to build, run, and test. A good README lets a new engineer go from a fresh laptop to a running service in under thirty minutes.

Runbooks answer "an alert just fired — what do I do right now?" A runbook is tied to a specific, named alert. For example, a runbook titled "DB connection pool exhausted" states the symptom the engineer will see, the likely causes in order of probability, the exact commands to confirm each cause, and the remediation steps. It ends with an escalation path: if these steps do not resolve it in fifteen minutes, page the database on-call. The key property is that a runbook is written for someone who did not build the system and is reading it under stress.

Troubleshooting guides answer "something is wrong but no single alert captures it." They are more open-ended than runbooks. A troubleshooting guide for a settlement service might explain how to trace a single trade through the logs using a correlation ID, how to check whether the problem is in this service or a downstream one, and which dashboards to open. Where a runbook is a straight line, a troubleshooting guide is a decision tree.

Deployment documentation answers "how do I ship a change safely and undo it if it goes wrong?" It covers the versioning scheme, the exact deploy command or pipeline stage, how to verify the deployment succeeded such as checking the health endpoint and a smoke-test transfer, and critically, how to roll back. In a bank, the rollback procedure is as important as the deploy procedure, because a bad release that moves money must be reversible in minutes.

Architecture diagrams answer "how does this service fit into the bigger picture?" A single page showing that the Transfer Service receives requests from the API Gateway, reads and writes PostgreSQL, publishes events to Kafka, and calls the Fraud Service lets a new on-call engineer reason about blast radius immediately.

The senior-level nuance is that runbooks are a reliability tool, not just paperwork. Mean Time To Recovery, or MTTR, is the average time from an incident starting to it being resolved. Runbooks directly shrink MTTR because the engineer does not spend the first thirty minutes rediscovering what someone already knew. They also reduce "tribal knowledge," which is dangerous knowledge that lives only in one person's head and walks out the door when that person leaves. Runbooks are validated by use: every incident is a chance to improve the runbook, and a mature team runs game-days where they deliberately trigger a failure to confirm the runbook actually works.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the Transfer Service moves money between accounts. It is backed by a PostgreSQL database and uses a HikariCP connection pool with a fixed maximum of ten connections. One evening, a batch job and heavy customer traffic together try to borrow more than ten connections at once.

Problem 1 — The service suddenly starts failing transfers with timeout errors. The on-call engineer, who did not build this service, sees an alert that says "DB connection pool exhausted." Without a runbook, this engineer would have to read the source code, find the pool size, guess at the cause, and perhaps restart the wrong thing. This is exactly the situation a runbook solves: a named alert maps to a written procedure that anyone can follow.

Problem 2 — To follow the procedure, the engineer needs to actually inspect the live pool: how many connections are active, how many are idle, and how many threads are waiting. A real service must expose this information. This is exactly how operational tooling works — the service publishes pool metrics that the runbook tells the engineer how to read.

Problem 3 — After confirming the cause, the engineer needs a safe remediation and a clear escalation point. This is exactly what the runbook's remediation and escalation sections provide, so the engineer acts decisively instead of experimenting on a production money-moving service.

To make this concrete and runnable, we will build a small program that simulates the Transfer Service and its connection pool. It will contain an `Account` class with debit and credit, a `ConnectionPool` class that models the HikariCP-style bounded pool with active, idle, and waiting counts, a `TransferService` that borrows a connection to perform a transfer, and a `PoolMetrics` reporter that prints exactly the numbers a runbook would ask the engineer to check. The demo will drive enough concurrent transfers to exhaust the pool, then print the metrics the runbook references, showing how documentation and tooling line up.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
server:
  port: 8080
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/bankdb
    username: transfer_app
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10        # the limit that gets exhausted in the scenario
      connection-timeout: 2000     # ms to wait for a connection before failing
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,metrics    # the runbook tells on-call to curl these
```

The runbook itself is an operational artifact and part of the deliverable:

```text
# Runbook: DB connection pool exhausted

SYMPTOM
- Alert "DB connection pool exhausted" fires.
- Transfers fail with "connection is not available, request timed out".

LIKELY CAUSES (most to least likely)
1. Traffic spike + batch job running at the same time.
2. A slow query holding connections for too long.
3. A connection leak (connections borrowed but never returned).

CONFIRM
- curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.active
- curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.pending
- If active == max and pending > 0 for minutes -> pool is exhausted.

REMEDIATE
1. Check if the nightly batch is running; if yes, pause it.
2. Identify slow queries: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state='active';
3. If a leak is suspected, rolling-restart the service (zero downtime).

ESCALATE
- If not resolved in 15 min, page the Database on-call.
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build the project
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -jar target/transfer-service-1.0.0.jar

# In production, the runbook tells on-call to read live metrics:
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.active
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.pending
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: fifty concurrent transfer requests, each moving 1000 rupees from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001), against a connection pool whose maximum size is ten.

Step 1: The demo submits fifty tasks to a thread pool. All fifty tasks try to start at roughly the same moment, and each one immediately calls `pool.borrow()`.

Step 2: The first ten tasks acquire a permit from the semaphore and move into the active state. The pool now reports ten active connections and zero idle connections.

Step 3: The remaining forty tasks find no free permit. They enter the waiting state and count up the `waiting` counter. At this instant the pool is exhausted: active equals the maximum of ten, and pending is forty.

Step 4: `metrics.report()` runs while the storm is in progress. It prints active equals ten, idle equals zero, and pending is greater than zero, then logs the warning that points the engineer to the runbook. This is exactly the signal the on-call engineer would see in production.

Step 5: Each active transfer finishes its simulated fifty-millisecond query, performs the debit and credit on the in-memory accounts, and then releases its permit in the finally block. As each permit is released, one waiting task wakes up and becomes active.

Step 6: Over several waves, all fifty transfers complete. Because the pool is bounded, the work is serialized in groups of ten rather than overwhelming the database.

Step 7: The second `metrics.report()` runs after the executor terminates. It now shows active equals zero and idle equals ten, confirming every connection was returned and there is no leak.

Final output:

```text

INFO: transfer 1000 SAV2001->CUR3001 OK
Oct 25, 2026 1:15:02 AM com.bank.transfer.ops.PoolMetrics report
INFO: hikaricp.connections.active  = 10
INFO: hikaricp.connections.idle    = 0
INFO: hikaricp.connections.pending = 40
Oct 25, 2026 1:15:02 AM com.bank.transfer.ops.PoolMetrics report
WARNING: POOL EXHAUSTED -> follow runbook db-connection-pool-exhausted.md
...
INFO: hikaricp.connections.active  = 0
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A production service needs five kinds of operational documentation, and each one answers a different practical question. The README orients a new engineer: what the service does, its key dependencies, and the exact commands to build, run, and test it locally. Runbooks answer "an alert just fired, what do I do now?" — each one is tied to a named alert and walks the reader through the symptom, how to confirm the cause, how to remediate, and when to escalate. Troubleshooting guides are the more open-ended cousin of runbooks, giving diagnostic recipes and decision trees for failures that no single alert captures. Deployment documentation covers how to release, how to verify success, and critically how to roll back. And architecture diagrams show how this service connects to the gateway, the database, the message broker, and downstream services so an engineer can reason about blast radius.

The part I always emphasise is that runbooks are a reliability tool, not paperwork. The metric that matters in operations is Mean Time To Recovery, the average time from an incident starting to it being fixed. A runbook shrinks that time dramatically because the on-call engineer does not spend the first thirty minutes rediscovering knowledge that already existed in someone's head. It also removes the danger of tribal knowledge, where only one person knows how to fix something and the system is fragile the moment they are unavailable. A good runbook lets any on-call engineer handle an incident they have never personally seen.

At National Bank of India, I wrote a runbook for our Transfer Service called "DB connection pool exhausted." It named the alert, told the engineer to curl the active and pending connection metrics, explained that active equal to the maximum with pending above zero means the pool is exhausted, and then listed remediation steps: pause the nightly batch, look for slow queries in the activity table, and rolling-restart if a leak is suspected. It ended with a fifteen-minute escalation rule to the database on-call. The first time that alert fired at night, an engineer who had never touched the service resolved it in under ten minutes just by following the page.

I treat documentation as a living artifact that lives in the repository beside the code and goes through the same pull-request review. Every incident is an opportunity to improve the relevant runbook, and a mature team periodically runs a game-day where they deliberately trigger a failure to prove the runbook actually works under pressure. In a regulated industry like banking, this discipline is not optional nicety — it is how you keep recovery fast, reduce dependence on any single person, and demonstrate to auditors that the team can operate the system responsibly.
